selected.sourceTitle: How Darin Epsilon’s workflow with Massive X and Monark keeps Perspectives Digital moving forward
selected.extractionSummary: This article is an interview with Darin Epsilon, founder of Perspectives Digital, discussing his 15-year evolution as a producer in the melodic house and techno space. He traces his workflow from early atmospheric tools (Absynth, Massive) to current instruments (Massive X, Monark), emphasizing how the genre's demands have shifted toward sharper transients, tighter low-end, and modulated lead lines. Key production insights include layering philosophy, subtle modulation depths (1–3%), and the complementary pairing of digital and analog-modeled synthesis. The article is a sponsored/promotional piece for Native Instruments rather than an academic source, so claims reflect practitioner knowledge and marketing framing.

claims.text: Very subtle modulation depth (1–3%) on parameters like filter cutoff or wavetable position can make a sound feel more alive without altering its core character.

citations.label: Epsilon modulation tip
citations.quote: try adding very subtle movement to just one or two parameters—like filter cutoff or wavetable position. Even a tiny modulation depth (1–3%) can make a lead or pad feel more alive without changing the core character of the sound.

claims.text: Modern melodic house and techno production demands sharper transients, tighter low-end control, and evolving modulated lead lines compared to earlier progressive house styles that relied on pads and slow-evolving atmospheres.

citations.label: Genre evolution description
citations.quote: the production style demands sharper transients, tighter low-end control, fewer atmospheric pads, and a greater emphasis on modulated, evolving lead lines that drive tension and emotion.

claims.text: When layering synthesizers, assigning each layer a single acoustic role (attack, body, movement, or air) produces cleaner mixes than using a single complex all-in-one patch.

citations.label: Layering philosophy
citations.quote: When layering synths, give each layer a single job — attack, body, movement, or air. Purpose-built layers glue together far more cleanly than 'big' all-in-one patches and make mixing easier.

claims.text: Running pads or drones through subtle saturation or tape-style effects adds dimension and warmth with less mix-muddying than heavy reverb application.

citations.label: Saturation vs reverb tip
citations.quote: Run pads or drones through Guitar Rig with very subtle saturation or tape-style effects. This adds dimension, presence, and warmth without relying on large amounts of reverb that can muddy the mix.

claims.text: Using pitched transitions (processed plucks, reversed leads, tonal sweeps) rather than generic noise risers creates smoother, more musical movement between song sections.

citations.label: Transition design tip
citations.quote: Instead of relying on generic noise risers, try using pitched elements – such as lightly processed plucks, reversed leads, or short tonal sweeps – to guide transitions. This creates smoother, more musical movement between sections.

claims.text: Pairing a steady foundational bass with a subtle higher-register secondary bass layer adds harmonic movement without destabilizing low-end.

citations.label: Bass layering tip
citations.quote: Pair a steady, foundational bass with a subtle, higher-register secondary bass layer that adds movement. This creates interest without compromising low-end stability.

claims.text: Listeners are increasingly drawn to music that incorporates micro-movement, organic imperfections, and evolving timbres, which modern synthesizers are now capable of producing.

citations.label: Listener perception speculation
citations.quote: listeners are gravitating toward music that feels human and expressive. Modern synths make it easier to create patches with micro-movement, organic imperfections, and evolving timbres that heighten emotional impact.

claims.text: Small, subtle emotional details in sound design—ones listeners may not consciously notice—are nonetheless felt and contribute to emotional impact on the dancefloor.

citations.label: Subliminal sound design claim
citations.quote: It helps me craft small emotional details that listeners might not explicitly notice, but they feel them.

selected.sourceTitle: Building dialogue in electronic music with Kontakt, Monark, and David Mayer
selected.extractionSummary: David Mayer discusses his production process for 'News Flash,' a track built around an Eastern-leaning lead sampled and manipulated in Kontakt. He describes a hybrid workflow combining Kontakt for textural, expressive realism and Monark for analog bass grit. Central to his compositional philosophy is the principle of 'call and response,' which he applies at the level of beats, melodic phrases, and arrangement sections. He also explores the tension between club functionality and symphonic layering, seeking to embed emotional complexity within dance music structures. The article is a promotional interview with Native Instruments and carries no academic or scientific rigor.

selected.sourceTitle: HHL with a Coherent Fourier Oracle: A Proof-of-Concept Quantum Architecture for Joint Melody-Harmony Generation
selected.extractionSummary: This preprint proposes a quantum computing architecture for joint melody and harmony generation using the HHL algorithm, encoding music-cognition models (Narmour implication-realisation and Krumhansl-Kessler tonal stability) into a sparse linear system whose solution vector represents a weighted note-pair distribution. A coherent Fourier harmonic oracle is introduced as a unitary operator that applies chord-transition weights to the HHL amplitude vector, enabling a single quantum measurement to jointly select melody notes and a two-chord progression. To manage state-space complexity, generation is limited to 2-note/2-chord blocks chained classically. A four-block chain demonstration yields 8 notes over 8 chords, with 97% of generated chord progressions rated grammatically strong or acceptable by an independent rule-based validator. The primary theoretical motivation is preserving HHL's exponential speedup over classical linear solvers by consuming the output coherently rather than reading it classically.

citations.label: Core theoretical claim about HHL speedup
citations.quote: The primary motivation is that HHL carries a proven exponential speedup over classical linear solvers; this work demonstrates that a coherent HHL+oracle pipeline - the prerequisite for that speedup to be realised in a musical setting - is mechanically achievable.

claims.text: Reading HHL output classically cancels the quantum speedup; the solution must be consumed coherently for the speedup to be realised.

citations.label: Coherence requirement for quantum speedup
citations.quote: The key constraint of HHL is that reading its output classically cancels the quantum speedup; the solution must be consumed coherently.

selected.sourceTitle: Cross-Linguistic Rhythmic and Spectral Feature-Based Analysis of Nyishi and Adi: Two Under-Resourced Languages of Arunachal Pradesh
selected.extractionSummary: This preprint investigates acoustic differentiation between two under-resourced Tani languages (Nyishi and Adi) spoken in Arunachal Pradesh using rhythm formant analysis (RFA) in the frequency domain. The study extracts low-frequency amplitude modulation features from speech signals to characterize speech rhythm, finding that Nyishi exhibits higher dominant modulation frequencies and greater dispersion than Adi. Combining rhythmic features with spectral features (MFCC) yields classification accuracies up to 93.96%, demonstrating that low-frequency modulation and spectral structure encode complementary and hierarchical levels of linguistic variation. The approach treats speech rhythm as a spectral phenomenon analyzable via amplitude modulation in the low-frequency range, which has direct relevance to acoustic and musical analysis frameworks.

selected.sourceTitle: ClariCodec: Optimising Neural Speech Codes for 200bps Communication using Reinforcement Learning
selected.extractionSummary: ClariCodec is a neural speech codec designed for ultra-low bitrate communication (200 bps) that uses reinforcement learning to optimize for speech intelligibility rather than acoustic reconstruction fidelity. The system reformulates quantization as a stochastic policy, allowing RL-based rewards driven by word error rate (WER) to fine-tune the encoder while keeping the acoustic reconstruction pipeline frozen. Without RL, it achieves 3.68% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean; with RL fine-tuning, WER drops to 3.20% (test-clean) and 8.93% (test-other), a 13% relative reduction. This work highlights a fundamental tension between perceptual detail and intelligibility at extreme compression ratios. The approach is relevant to acoustics and audio engineering communities interested in how speech information is prioritized under severe bandwidth constraints.

selected.sourceTitle: WST-X Series: Wavelet Scattering Transform for Interpretable Speech Deepfake Detection
selected.extractionSummary: This paper proposes WST-X, a feature extraction system for detecting AI-generated (deepfake) speech using the Wavelet Scattering Transform (WST). The WST cascades wavelet convolutions with modulus nonlinearities to produce deformation-stable, multi-scale acoustic representations. The authors find that small temporal averaging scales combined with high frequency and directional resolution are critical for capturing subtle spectral artifacts in synthetic speech. WST-X outperforms both hand-crafted filterbank features and self-supervised learning (SSL) features on multiple benchmarks. The work sits at the intersection of signal processing, acoustics, and machine learning.

selected.sourceTitle: StreamMark: A Deep Learning-Based Semi-Fragile Audio Watermarking for Proactive Deepfake Detection
selected.extractionSummary: StreamMark is a deep learning-based audio watermarking system designed for proactive deepfake audio detection. It embeds imperceptible watermarks into audio that survive benign transformations (compression, noise) but break under semantics-altering manipulations like voice conversion or speech editing. The system operates in the complex frequency domain using an Encoder-Distortion-Decoder architecture. Benchmarks show high audio quality preservation (SNR 24.16 dB, PESQ 4.20) and near-chance watermark recovery (~50% accuracy) after deepfake attacks, while maintaining >98% accuracy after benign transformations. The work is directly relevant to the question of how audio signals encode and preserve meaning across transformations.

selected.sourceTitle: Do LLM Decoders Listen Fairly? Benchmarking How Language Model Priors Shape Bias in Speech Recognition
selected.extractionSummary: This paper benchmarks speech recognition fairness across demographic groups using nine models and ~43,000 utterances. It finds that LLM-based decoders do not amplify racial bias and may outperform older architectures on ethnicity fairness. Critically, audio encoder design — not language model scale — is identified as the primary driver of both bias and robustness. Acoustic degradation conditions reveal pathological hallucination and repetition behaviors in certain architectures, particularly Whisper on accented or silence-injected speech.

selected.sourceTitle: DeepForestSound: a multi-species automatic detector for passive acoustic monitoring in African tropical forests, a case study in Kibale National Park
selected.extractionSummary: DeepForestSound (DFS) is a machine learning model for passive acoustic monitoring in African tropical forests, specifically Kibale National Park, Uganda. It uses a semi-supervised pipeline combining unsupervised clustering of unannotated recordings with supervised fine-tuning of an Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST) via low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The model detects multiple taxonomic groups — birds, primates, and elephants — from long-term field recordings. DFS achieves high average precision (0.964 for primates, 0.961 for elephants) and outperforms general-purpose ecoacoustic models on underrepresented taxa. The study demonstrates that region-specific, task-oriented acoustic training substantially improves performance in acoustically complex tropical environments.
